title: JetSpec: Breaking the Scaling Ceiling of Speculative Decoding
hook: Speculative decoding stalls when bigger draft trees stop paying off. JetSpec trains a causal parallel draft head that drafts in one pass yet stays branch-consistent — hitting up to 9.64x speedup.
key_points: Speculative decoding speeds LLMs by drafting several tokens, then verifying them in parallel — but gains plateau as draft budgets grow.
The dilemma: autoregressive drafters give consistent trees but cost grows with depth; one-pass diffusion drafters are cheap but produce mutually inconsistent candidates.
JetSpec trains a causal parallel draft head over the frozen target model's fused hidden states, so drafts align with the target's own factorization.
This turns larger draft budgets into longer accepted prefixes instead of wasted compute.
Reports up to 9.64x speedup on MATH-500 and 4.58x on open-ended chat on H100 GPUs, with vLLM integration.
content_html: Speculative decoding makes LLMs faster by having a cheap drafter propose several tokens that the big model verifies in parallel. JetSpec tackles why throwing more draft budget at the problem eventually stops helping.
extra_html:
The dilemma

Bigger draft trees only help if the target model accepts most of them and the drafting itself stays cheap. Prior methods sit on the wrong side of a trade-off. Autoregressive drafters produce path-conditioned candidates with good acceptance, but their cost grows with tree depth. Bidirectional block-diffusion drafters generate all positions in one pass, but their branch-agnostic predictions can form trees that are individually plausible yet mutually inconsistent — wasting budget and lowering acceptance.

JetSpec's fix

JetSpec trains a causal parallel draft head over fused hidden states from the frozen target model. It drafts in a single forward pass (cheap), yet scores candidates so they align with the target model's own autoregressive factorization (consistent). That lets larger draft budgets convert into longer accepted prefixes rather than discarded guesses. On H100 GPUs across math, coding, and chat with Qwen3 models, the authors report up to 9.64x speedup on MATH-500 and 4.58x on conversational workloads, plus end-to-end gains under realistic serving via vLLM. Code is linked from the paper.
